keyPoints: Chapter 9
Designing Runtime Polymorphism
Modern C++ lecture with code, output, and presenter script
slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 9: Designing Runtime Polymorphism. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Designing Runtime Polymorphism changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 9, treat 9.1.2 Understanding Dynamic Dispatch as a design decision with costs and evidence. Calling accepts through a Filter* or reference dispatches according to the actual derived object. Implementations commonly use virtual tables, but the language contract does not require one fixed object layout or forbid devirtualization when the optimizer knows the target. Dispatch is not ownership. A borrowed base reference does not keep the object alive, and an owning base pointer needs a correct destruction interface. Do not measure one indirect call and assume it describes the complete cost of the design; allocation patterns, data locality, and work performed by the predicate can dominate. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 9, treat 9.2.2 Using Virtual Destructors Safely as a design decision with costs and evidence. The interface has virtual ~Filter() = default;, permitting correct destruction when an owning base pointer refers to a derived object. The vector stores std::unique_ptr<Filter>, so clearing it deletes through the base interface and must invoke the appropriate derived destruction. Avoid object slicing: storing a derived object by value in a base-valued collection would keep only the base portion, and an abstract base cannot serve that purpose at all. Polymorphic objects are commonly accessed through references or pointers whose owners are explicit. Copying a polymorphic value, when needed, requires a deliberate cloning or value-wrapper design rather than an accidental base copy. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 9, treat Separate dispatch from ownership as a design decision with costs and evidence. The vector owns unique pointers, and each pointer owns one concrete filter. The call through filters[0] reaches the minimum-value policy; the call through filters[1] reaches the parity policy. The application does not downcast to identify which class it received. It depends only on the accepts contract. Clearing the vector releases the owning pointers and destroys the complete filters through their virtual base destructors. The test checks that the vector is empty afterward. A deeper cleanup test can add a resource-audit member to each concrete implementation and verify that all acquired resources are released. slides.title: Failure clinic — The almost-matching override
keyPoints: A derived class writes bool accepts(int) while the base declares bool accepts(int) const.
Without override, the code can introduce a different member and leave the class abstract or preserve an unexpected.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 9, treat Failure clinic — The almost-matching override as a design decision with costs and evidence. A derived class writes bool accepts(int) while the base declares bool accepts(int) const. Without override, the code can introduce a different member and leave the class abstract or preserve an unexpected base implementation in a different hierarchy. With override, the compiler points directly at the mismatch. The correction is to match the intended interface, not to remove override to silence the diagnostic. Another defect stores derived values in a vector<Base>. In a concrete base hierarchy this can slice each value, losing derived behavior. A vector of owning base pointers preserves the dynamic objects but changes the copy and allocation model. A variant can be an alternative when the set of implementations is closed and known at compile time. Chapter 19 develops that tradeoff rather than presenting inheritance as the only way to represent alternatives. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.
